titleText.es: Nuestros cerebros solo tienen una escala y lo que hacemos es redimensionar nuestras experiencias para que encajen.
titleText.en: Our brains have just one scale, and we resize our experiences to fit.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish and official title attributes are preserved exactly. Vision split SOPORTAR, PROBADO, CUALQUIERA, FOTOGRAMAS, ABURRIDOS, and ALABANDO at genuine printed line wraps; each is one lexical occurrence. It also omitted several third-panel and lower-panel words and misread accents, letters, the Wikipedia name, and the abbreviated frame labels. WIKIPEDIA, JOE BIDEN, J.B., and the four numeric labels are audited exclusions.

regions.labelEs: ¿CÓMO PUEDES SOPORTAR ESTE VINO BARATO? A MÍ TODOS LOS VINOS ME SABEN IGUAL.

applications.explanationEn: Cómo keeps its written accent because it directly asks how the action is possible.
Puedes supplies the ability form and soportar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
The descriptive adjective barato follows the noun vino.
Barato uses masculine singular form to agree with vino.
A mí states and emphasizes the person who experiences the taste.
Me remains before the taste verb and matches the emphasized experiencer mí.
Saben is the finite verb whose experiencer is marked by me and clarified by a mí.

applications.exampleEs: A MÍ TODOS LOS VINOS ME SABEN IGUAL
applications.explanationEn: Plural vinos controls saben; a mí and me identify the experiencer, and igual supplies the taste judgment.

regions.labelEs: ESO ES PORQUE NUNCA HAS PROBADO BUEN VINO. SI PRESTARAS MÁS ATENCIÓN, VERÍAS QUE ESTO ES TODO UN MUNDO.

applications.explanationEn: Has is the helper used with informal tú, and probado presents the experience as completed.
Bueno shortens to buen directly before the masculine singular noun vino.
Si introduces the imagined condition without an accent.
Prestaras is the -ra form used for the hypothetical condition.
Prestar and atención form the expression for paying attention; más states the degree.
Verías is the conditional form that gives the imagined result.
Ver keeps its irregular stem ver- and adds -ías for the conditional.
Todo intensifies un mundo as a rich subject in its own right.

regions.labelEs: ¡PERO ESO ES CIERTO PARA CUALQUIER COSA! VINO, MÚSICA HOUSE, TIPOS DE LETRA, HORMIGAS, FIRMAS DE LA WIKIPEDIA, PORNO CANADIENSE SURREALISTA... DEDÍCALE TIEMPO A CUALQUIERA DE ESTAS COSAS Y TE CONVERTIRÁS EN UN CONNOISSEUR ESNOB.

excludedUnits.rationale: This encyclopedia brand name is a proper product name rather than Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Cualquier keeps its shortened form directly before the singular noun cosa.
Plural tipos combines with de letra to name multiple typefaces.
Both descriptive adjectives follow the noun porno.
The descriptions stay singular to agree with singular porno.
Dedica is the affirmative command used with one familiar listener.
Le attaches to the affirmative tú command, and the written accent preserves the original stress.

applications.exampleEs: DEDÍCALE TIEMPO A CUALQUIERA DE ESTAS COSAS
applications.explanationEn: Dedícale and tiempo state the commitment, while a introduces any one of the listed targets.

applications.exampleEs: TE CONVERTIRÁS EN UN CONNOISSEUR ESNOB
applications.explanationEn: Te convertirás gives the future change, en introduces the resulting identity, and the final noun phrase names it.
Convertir keeps its whole dictionary form and adds -ás for informal singular future.
The descriptive adjective esnob follows the noun connoisseur.
Esnob stays singular to agree with the singular noun.

regions.labelEs: PERO ALGUNAS COSAS TIENEN MÁS PROFUNDIDAD QUE OTRAS. SI METES A GENTE EN UNA CAJA DURANTE UN AÑO CON 500 FOTOGRAMAS DE JOE BIDEN COMIÉNDOSE UN SÁNDWICH, AL FINAL ESTARÁN CONVENCIDOS DE QUE ALGUNOS SON GENIALES Y OTROS SON HORRIBLES. EXAGERAS. ¿TÚ CREES?

excludedUnits.rationale: This printed quantity is a numeral rather than a Spanish lexical word.
This two-word personal name is a proper name rather than Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Más raises the degree of profundidad, and que introduces the comparison.
Si introduces a condition presented as possible.
Metes is the ordinary present form used in the possible condition.
A marks the person-denoting object gente.
Se presents the eating as consumption of the specified item.
Al final marks the eventual outcome.
Estarán states the future result of the earlier si condition.
Estar keeps its whole dictionary form and adds -án for a plural future subject.
Estarán and plural convencidos describe the group, while de que introduces its belief.
Tú is stated to contrast or challenge the other speaker's judgment.
Question marks and intonation turn tú crees into a yes-or-no question without an extra helper.

regions.labelEs: —UN AÑO DESPUÉS— ES CIERTO, LA MAYORÍA DE LOS FOTOGRAMAS DE BOCA CERRADA SON ABURRIDOS, PERO EN EL N° 415, LA FORMA EN LA QUE LA MANDÍBULA ENMARCA LA MAYONESA DE SU MANO ES PURA PERFECCIÓN, Y...

excludedUnits.rationale: This printed item number is a numeral label rather than Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: The time span un año comes before después.
La mayoría de introduces most members of the complete group los fotogramas.
The descriptive adjective cerrada follows the noun boca.
Cerrada uses feminine singular form to agree with boca.
En comes before la que, whose feminine article matches the earlier forma.
The evaluative intensifier pura comes before the abstract noun perfección.
Pura uses feminine singular form to agree with perfección.

regions.labelEs: OH, QUÉ NOVEDAD, TÚ ALABANDO UN FOTOGRAMA CON MAYONESA. AL ESCUCHARTE, CUALQUIERA DIRÍA QUE NO EXISTE NADA MÁS EN EL SÁNDWICH.

applications.explanationEn: Accented qué comes directly before the noun novedad to form an exclamation.
Al plus the unchanged infinitive expresses what happens upon hearing the person.
Te attaches to escuchar as one written word.
Decir uses the irregular conditional stem dir- plus -ía.
No precedes the verb and nada follows it, forming normal Spanish negative concord.

regions.labelEs: FRANCAMENTE, TAL Y COMO DA LA LUZ EN EL CUELLO DE J.B. A TRAVÉS DE LA LECHUGA EN LA N°. 242, LA COLOCARÍA EN MI TOP 10 AUNQUE NO TUVIERA NINGUNA MAYONESA EN SU MANO.

excludedUnits.rationale: This abbreviated personal name is an identifier rather than Spanish vocabulary.
This printed frame number is a numeral label rather than Spanish vocabulary.
This ranking number is a numeral rather than a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Franca takes -mente to form the adverb francamente.
Tal y como introduces the exact manner being described.
A, través, and de form the fixed expression for a path through something.
Colocar keeps its whole dictionary form and adds -ía for the imagined ranking.
Aunque introduces the concession, and tuviera gives its unreal -ra condition.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?
Why do the characters develop elaborate judgments about nearly identical images?
cards.answerEn: Sustained attention creates expertise and a finer internal scale, even when the subject initially seems shallow or arbitrary.
cards.noteEn: The joke begins with a claim that careful attention reveals a whole world in any subject. An artificial year-long exposure to near-identical sandwich images then produces confident aesthetic distinctions, parodying both genuine expertise and snobbery.

example.es: Con práctica, una persona distingue matices que antes parecían iguales.
example.en: With practice, a person distinguishes nuances that once seemed identical.

cards.answerEn: you can; you are able to

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.
This sense of soportar is about tolerating something unpleasant, not physically supporting weight.

example.en: I cannot put up with that noise.

cards.noteEn: Vino is the masculine noun for wine. The same written form can also be a past form of venir, but a drink or packaging context identifies the noun.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Barato describes a masculine singular thing with a low price.

cards.answerEn: to; for (introducing whose tastes are described)
cards.noteEn: With the informal preference use of ir, a can introduce the person whose tastes are described; a short word such as le normally repeats that person before the verb.

example.es: A Daniel le van los deportes.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish emphasize the person who experiences a feeling, preference, or taste?
cards.answerEn: Add a plus the person for emphasis or clarification, while keeping the matching small pronoun before the verb.
cards.noteEn: The a phrase clarifies or contrasts the experiencer; it does not replace me, te, le, nos, os, or les.

example.es: A mí me gusta el té.

cards.questionEn: How does saber express how food or drink tastes to someone?
cards.answerEn: Name the food or drink, use the matching small experiencer pronoun plus a form of saber, and add the taste description.
cards.noteEn: The thing tasted controls singular sabe or plural saben. The pronoun identifies who experiences the taste.

example.es: A Marta, las aceitunas le saben saladas.
example.en: To Marta, the olives taste salty.

cards.answerEn: me (after a preposition such as para)
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses mí after most prepositions. The written accent distinguishes mí (“me”) from mi (“my”).
Vinos is the plural of vino.

example.es: La tienda vende vinos de varias regiones.
example.en: The shop sells wines from several regions.

cards.answerEn: to me; marks the person who experiences a taste
cards.noteEn: With saber in its taste sense, me identifies the speaker as the person to whom something tastes a certain way.

example.en: The tea tastes sweet to me.

cards.noteEn: Saben is a plural present form of saber. With a taste description, saber means “to taste,” not “to know.”
Igual can describe two or more experiences as the same.

example.en: The two versions sound the same.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Probado is probar's completed-action form. After a form of haber, it asks or states whether an option has been tried.

example.en: Have you all tried another solution?

cards.noteEn: Bueno shortens to buen directly before a masculine singular noun.

cards.promptEs: bueno → buen delante de un sustantivo masculino singular
cards.questionEn: Why does bueno sometimes appear as buen?
cards.answerEn: Shorten bueno to buen when it comes directly before a masculine singular noun.
cards.noteEn: Use un buen libro but el libro es bueno. The shortening happens only before a masculine singular noun. Before a feminine noun, use buena, as in una buena idea; in plural, use buenos or buenas.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe an imagined “if…, …would…” situation?
cards.answerEn: Use si followed by a hypothetical past verb form for the condition, and use a “would” form for the result.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls the condition's verb form the imperfect subjunctive. It often ends in -ra or -se, as in tuviera or tuviese. The result uses the conditional, often ending in -ría, as in haría. In this pattern, do not put the conditional directly after si.

example.en: If I had time, I would travel more.

cards.noteEn: Prestaras is the -ra form used for an imagined condition. In prestar atención, prestar means “to pay.”

example.en: If you paid attention, you would remember more.

cards.noteEn: English uses “pay,” but Spanish uses prestar, a verb that by itself often means “to lend.” Add a before the person or thing receiving the attention: prestar atención a algo.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “to pay attention” in Spanish?

cards.noteEn: Verías is ver with the conditional ending -ías.

example.es: Con más luz, verías el detalle.
example.en: With more light, you would see the detail.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.
Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.
Before el plus a masculine singular noun, todo means the whole amount or extent of it: todo el día, todo el trabajo.

cards.questionEn: How can you describe a subject as a whole rich world of its own?
cards.noteEn: Todo adds an emphatic “whole” sense before un mundo.

example.es: La astronomía es todo un mundo.
example.en: Astronomy is a whole world of its own.

cards.noteEn: After es, cierto describes a statement or claim as true.
Para can introduce the subject or case to which a statement applies.

example.es: La regla es válida para cualquier caso.
example.en: The rule is valid for any case.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “any” before one singular thing?
cards.answerEn: Put cualquier before a singular noun: cualquier libro, cualquier opción.
cards.noteEn: A noun is a naming word such as libro or opción. Before a noun, cualquiera shortens to cualquier. The noun stays singular even when the meaning is any one out of many. The plus sign in the Spanish prompt means “followed by.”
House is an internationally used name for a style of electronic dance music.

cards.questionEn: What is the common Spanish expression for a typeface or font?
cards.noteEn: Tipo can change to plural tipos when more than one typeface is meant.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’
In tipo de letra, letra refers to the visual design used for written characters.

example.es: Elige un tipo de letra sencillo.

cards.noteEn: Firmas is the plural of firma.
Porno is a common shortened form of pornografía.
Canadiense has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns.
Surrealista has the same form with masculine and feminine singular nouns.

cards.answerEn: devote time to it or them (informal command)
cards.noteEn: Dedica is the affirmative tú command of dedicar, and attached le represents the target receiving the time or attention.

example.en: Devote an hour to the project.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?

cards.promptEs: dedicar tiempo a + persona, cosa o actividad
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone devotes time to a person, thing, or activity?
cards.answerEn: Use dedicar tiempo a, followed by the target.
cards.noteEn: The form of dedicar changes with the subject and time. A introduces what receives the time.

example.en: I devote time to learning languages.

cards.answerEn: to; introduces what time, effort, or a life is devoted to
cards.noteEn: Dedicar links the thing being devoted to its purpose or recipient with a. In a question, that a can move to the front with qué.

example.es: Dedico una hora a la lectura.
example.en: I devote an hour to reading.

cards.noteEn: Cualquiera can stand alone for any one person or thing in a stated group.

example.es: Puedes elegir cualquiera de estas rutas.
example.en: You can choose any one of these routes.

cards.answerEn: of; links one member to a larger group
cards.noteEn: After uno or una, de introduces the group that the one member belongs to.

example.en: He is one of my neighbors.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks a “you” verb used with te
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs use te when the person affected is the informal listener. The meaning belongs to the whole verb pattern, so English may not translate te separately.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something becomes or turns into something else?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of convertirse, then en, then name the result.
cards.noteEn: Convertirse is used with a matching short word such as me, te, se, or nos. Change convertir to match the person, thing, and time, but keep en before the resulting identity or form: se convierte en, se convirtió en, or se está convirtiendo en.

example.es: La oruga se convierte en mariposa.
example.en: The caterpillar turns into a butterfly.

cards.answerEn: you will become; you will turn into
cards.noteEn: Convertirás is the future form used for one familiar listener; with te and en it expresses becoming.

example.es: Con práctica, te convertirás en experta.
example.en: With practice, you will become an expert.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

cards.answerEn: into; introduces the result after convertirse
cards.noteEn: After convertirse, en links the changing person or thing to what it becomes. Keep en even though English may simply use become before a noun.

example.es: El agua se convierte en hielo.

cards.noteEn: Connoisseur is a borrowed noun for someone with refined knowledge and judgment in a field.
Esnob can be a noun or an adjective for someone who displays supposedly superior taste.

cards.questionEn: How do you compare an amount or degree as more than another?
cards.answerEn: Put más before the amount or degree and que before the comparison.
cards.noteEn: The compared content can be stated after más or understood from context. Que introduces the person, thing, time, or earlier standard used for comparison.

example.en: Now I read more than before.

cards.noteEn: Profundidad can be physical depth or the amount of complexity and richness in a subject.

example.en: The essay has a lot of depth.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what will happen if a real possibility occurs?
cards.answerEn: Use si with an ordinary present-time verb form for the condition, then state the result with a future form.
cards.noteEn: Si introduces a condition treated as genuinely possible. Spanish normally keeps the verb immediately after si in the present form, not the future. The result can use the future, built here by keeping the action verb and adding an ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.

example.en: If you finish early, we will have dinner together.

cards.noteEn: Metes is the informal singular present form of meter.

example.es: Metes los libros en una caja.
example.en: You put the books in a box.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a person-denoting object
cards.noteEn: The personal a also appears before words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) when they directly receive an action, even though they do not identify one specific individual.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.
Durante introduces a period of time. Natural English often uses ‘for’ before a measured duration, such as an hour, but ‘during’ before a named event or period, such as the meeting.
A fotograma is one still image in a film, animation, or video sequence.

example.es: El vídeo tiene treinta fotogramas por segundo.
example.en: The video has thirty frames per second.

cards.noteEn: Comiendo is the ongoing-action form of comer, and se can emphasize consuming the item completely.

example.es: El niño está comiéndose una manzana.
example.en: The child is eating an apple.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish emphasize reading, eating, or drinking a whole, clearly specified thing?
cards.answerEn: Choose me, te, se, nos, os, or se to match the person doing the action, and use it with the reading, eating, or drinking verb.
cards.noteEn: These small words can present the action as carried through over the complete book, meal, drink, or stated amount; they do not mean that the person acts on themselves. Compare leer un libro, “read a book,” with leerse un libro, which often suggests reading it through. The small word normally goes before a verb form that shows person and time, as in se leyó; it attaches to an unchanged dictionary form, as in leerse. This completion nuance is not required every time.

example.es: Ana se leyó la novela en dos días.
example.en: Ana read through the novel in two days.

cards.noteEn: The written accent keeps the stress on the first syllable.

cards.answerEn: in the; part of al final (“in the end”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say “in the end” or “eventually”?
cards.noteEn: Al final can name the literal end of something or the eventual outcome after events have unfolded.

example.en: In the end, we decided to stay.

cards.noteEn: Estarán is the third-person plural future form of estar.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce something that a person is convinced is true?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of estar convencido, then de que, then the belief.
cards.noteEn: Convencido changes to match the person or group described.

example.en: We are convinced that it will work.

cards.noteEn: Convencidos describes a masculine or mixed plural group that firmly believes something.

example.en: They are convinced that it will work.

cards.answerEn: of; no separate English word before que after convencido
cards.noteEn: Convencido requires de before a noun or before que plus the belief.

example.en: I am convinced that she will come.

cards.noteEn: Geniales has one form for masculine and feminine plural subjects.
Horribles has one form for masculine and feminine plural subjects.
Exageras is the informal singular present form of exagerar.

example.en: I think you are exaggerating the problem.

cards.questionEn: Why might Spanish say tú or yo when the verb already tells you who acts?
cards.answerEn: Say the subject pronoun to add emphasis, contrast, or clarity; otherwise Spanish often leaves it out.
cards.noteEn: A verb form such as eres already points to “you.” Adding tú can stress that particular person, especially in a contrast or a surprised question. The pronoun may appear after the verb.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens a stated amount of time later?
cards.answerEn: Put the length of time before después.
cards.noteEn: The duration comes first: tres días después means “three days later.” This differs from después de tres días, which presents the same duration after después and means “after three days.”

example.es: Tres días después, llegó la carta.
example.en: Three days later, the letter arrived.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to most members of a group?
cards.answerEn: Use la mayoría de, followed by the group.
cards.noteEn: The following noun phrase names the complete group from which the majority is taken.

example.es: La mayoría de los trenes llegó a tiempo.
example.en: Most of the trains arrived on time.

cards.noteEn: La mayoría de introduces the larger part of a group.

example.es: La mayoría de los alumnos llegó temprano.
example.en: Most of the students arrived early.

cards.noteEn: Boca names the mouth as a body part.
Cerrada is the feminine singular completed-action form used as a description.
Aburridos describes masculine plural things that cause boredom.

cards.questionEn: How do you say forms such as “in which,” “with whom,” or “for whom” when referring back to a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Put the needed preposition before el que, la que, los que, or las que, matching the earlier person or thing.
cards.noteEn: A preposition is a short relationship word such as en (“in”), con (“with”), or para (“for”). Choose el, la, los, or las to match the gender and number of the person or thing being described; que itself does not change. English may use “which” for a thing or “who” or “whom” for a person.

example.es: Esta es la silla en la que me siento.
example.en: This is the chair that I sit in.

cards.answerEn: the feminine article in la que; helps mean which, who, or whom

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Mandíbula is the lower or upper bony structure that holds the teeth.
Enmarca is the present form for one thing that surrounds or visually highlights another.
Mayonesa is the standard Spanish word for mayonnaise.

example.en: She added mayonnaise to the sandwich.

cards.noteEn: Su agrees with the possessed thing, not with the owner. The same Spanish form can mean his, her, its, their, or formal your; the surrounding context identifies the owner.
Mano is feminine despite ending in -o, so it takes una and feminine describing forms.
Before an abstract noun, puro or pura can intensify it with the sense “sheer” or “nothing but.”

cards.questionEn: Where do common judgment words such as bueno or malo often go?
cards.answerEn: Put them before the noun when they give an overall evaluation: buena idea, mala noticia.
cards.noteEn: Spanish often puts a neutral descriptive word after its noun, but common evaluation words can come before it. The describing word still changes to match the noun: bueno becomes buena before a feminine singular noun.

cards.answerEn: what a; what (before a noun in an exclamation)
cards.noteEn: Qué keeps its accent when it introduces an exclamation such as ¡qué sorpresa!

cards.questionEn: How do you exclaim about a person, thing, or situation named by a noun?
cards.answerEn: Put accented qué directly before the noun and use exclamation marks.
cards.noteEn: No article is inserted between qué and the noun.
Novedad names something new or unexpected; it can also appear sarcastically in an exclamation.

example.es: Esa noticia no es ninguna novedad.

cards.noteEn: Alabando is the ongoing-action form of alabar.

example.es: Siguió alabando el trabajo del equipo.
example.en: She kept praising the team's work.

cards.noteEn: A fotograma is one still image in a film, animation, or video sequence.

example.en: They analyzed every frame of the video.

cards.answerEn: Use al followed by the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Al + verb tells when the main action happens. Translate it naturally as “when,” “on,” or “upon”: al llegar means “when arriving” or simply “when someone arrives.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say “when doing something” or “upon doing something”?

example.en: When I arrive, I will call you.

cards.answerEn: to listen to you; to hear you
cards.noteEn: Escuchar stays in its dictionary form and te attaches to represent one familiar listener.

example.en: On listening to you, I understood the problem.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.
Diría is the conditional form of decir for I, he, she, or formal you.

example.en: I would say that it is enough.

cards.questionEn: Why can a Spanish sentence contain both no and another negative word?
cards.answerEn: When the second negative word follows the verb, keep no before the verb too.
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses matching negative words together. No tiene ninguna means “it does not have any”; it does not become a positive meaning as two negatives sometimes do in formal English.

example.en: I do not have any doubt.

cards.noteEn: After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.
Francamente is an adverb formed from franca plus -mente.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

cards.answerEn: just; exactly (as part of tal y como)
cards.noteEn: Tal is part of the fixed connector tal y como here. Learn the three words together as “just as” or “exactly as.”

example.en: It happened exactly as you said.

cards.questionEn: How do you emphasize that something is exactly as someone said, expected, or described?
cards.answerEn: Use tal y como before the description: it means “just as” or “exactly as.”
cards.noteEn: Treat tal y como as one connector here; tal and y do not need separate literal translations. What follows states the expectation or description being matched.

example.es: Todo ocurrió tal y como dijiste.
example.en: Everything happened exactly as you said.

cards.noteEn: Dar can describe light striking or falling on a place.

example.es: La luz da en la pared.
example.en: The light falls on the wall.

cards.noteEn: Cuello names the body part between the head and torso.

example.es: Lleva una bufanda en el cuello.
example.en: She wears a scarf around her neck.

cards.answerEn: belonging to; often expressed with ’s in English
cards.noteEn: De can connect a thing to its owner. Spanish says el libro de Ana where English can say ‘Ana’s book.’

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; part of a través de (“through”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something goes or can be seen through something?
cards.answerEn: Use a través de before the thing: it means “through” or “across.”
cards.noteEn: Keep all three parts together. Before masculine singular el, de and el combine as del: a través del bosque. Before a feminine noun, use a través de la, as in a través de la ventana. The expression can describe literal passage or a figurative means.

example.es: La luz entra a través de la ventana.
example.en: The light comes in through the window.

cards.answerEn: part of a través de, “through” or “across”
no separate English word; completes a través de, “through”

cards.noteEn: Lechuga is the leafy vegetable lettuce.

example.en: He put lettuce in the salad.

cards.noteEn: Colocaría is the conditional form of colocar for I, he, she, or formal you. In a list, it can mean “would rank.”

example.es: Yo la colocaría entre las mejores.
example.en: I would rank it among the best.

cards.noteEn: Top is a common loanword for the highest positions in a ranking.

example.es: La canción entró en el top diez.
example.en: The song entered the top ten.

cards.questionEn: How do you present a concession based on an unreal or counterfactual situation?
cards.answerEn: Use aunque followed by the special past-looking subjunctive form in -ra or -se.
cards.noteEn: This pattern says the main result would hold even under the imagined condition.

example.en: I would go even if it rained.

cards.noteEn: Tuviera is a special past form of tener used when the thing being described is sought, imagined, uncertain, or otherwise not presented as an established fact. For example, buscar una casa que tuviera jardín seeks a house with that feature rather than stating that a known house has it.

example.es: Buscaba una casa que tuviera jardín.
example.en: She was looking for a house that had a garden.
